about: Companion plugins claude-pipeline can suggest. Only ids listed here can ever be installed by toolkit.mjs. alwaysOnTokens = input tokens added to every session; measured = read from `claude plugin details` or an A/B run; detailsUndercounts marks plugins whose hooks or MCP tools add more than `claude plugin details` reports. headless = whether the pipeline's own headless steps may load it: 'off' means the runner always switches it off there.

presets.recommended: Smallest set that improves this pipeline: less code and output (ponytail) plus the skills the Plan, Build and Review steps use (agent-skills).
presets.full: Everything compatible, for people who do not want to choose. Adds session memory and context-window protection; costs several thousand extra tokens in every interactive session.

plugins.title: ponytail
plugins.does: Makes the AI write the least code that works: YAGNI, standard library first, no speculative abstractions.
plugins.forPipeline: Smaller diffs and less output in Build (fewer output tokens), and ponytail-review hunts over-engineering in Review.

plugins.title: agent-skills
plugins.does: 25 engineering skills covering spec, plan, build, test, review, security, performance and launch, plus reviewer personas.
plugins.forPipeline: Supplies the skills the steps invoke: planning-and-task-breakdown, test-driven-development, code-review-and-quality, security-and-hardening.
notes: Also counts as installed when its skills are copied into ~/.claude/skills.

plugins.title: context-mode
plugins.does: Keeps big tool output (web pages, logs, large files, Playwright snapshots) out of the conversation: code runs in a sandbox and only the answer comes back, with a searchable local index and session recovery after compaction.
plugins.forPipeline: Best for the long interactive sessions where you research or debug with large outputs. The pipeline keeps it OFF inside its own headless steps.
notes: `claude plugin details` shows only ~631 tokens because hook-injected instructions and MCP tool schemas are not counted; the A/B run counts everything.
Measured here with Haiku on tiny tasks: +8.6K input tokens per session, and no saving when tool output is small. Its benefit appears with large outputs.

Observed side effect: on its first start it writes a self-heal hook into ~/.claude/hooks/ and ~/.claude/settings.json and adds itself to enabledPlugins. On native Windows that hook printed a PowerShell ParserError at every session start. Know this before installing.
Elastic License 2.0: source-available, free to use yourself, not OSI open source (you may not resell it as a hosted service).
Adds an MCP server and hooks that route or block some Bash, Read, Grep and WebFetch calls; the first start runs npm install for a native SQLite module (about 20 s).
Stores its index and session events locally in ~/.context-mode; its README states nothing leaves your machine (the optional ctx-insight command opens a hosted dashboard).
setup: After restarting Claude Code, run /context-mode:ctx-doctor: every check should pass.

plugins.title: agentmemory
plugins.does: Remembers decisions, gotchas and lessons across sessions, and resumes where you stopped (/handoff, /recall, /remember, /lesson).
plugins.forPipeline: Saves each milestone's outcome and your corrections, so the next session starts informed. The headless steps do not need it.
notes: The listed tokens are a floor: its MCP tool schemas are not counted by `claude plugin details`.
Needs its local memory server running: npx -y @agentmemory/agentmemory@latest. On native Windows the engine (iii.exe v0.11.2) must be installed once by hand; WSL2 or Docker also work. See its README.
setup: Start the server in a terminal: npx -y @agentmemory/agentmemory@latest
Native Windows: install iii.exe v0.11.2 first (see the agentmemory README, section Windows).

plugins.title: superpowers
plugins.does: A complete development methodology: brainstorm, plan, subagent-driven build, review, with git worktree isolation.
plugins.forPipeline: An alternative to agent-skills for long autonomous runs. Use one or the other: two routers on the same task fight over commands and TDD style.
